- **Net cash on a net-debt basis:** "Net debt is minus 45." Gross debt INR840cr vs "580 odd crores" at March, entirely
  explained by the final TBM instalment; guided "less than INR800 crores by the year end, not more" as term loan
  amortises.
- **Leverage:** "Gross debt equity is at 0.24."
- **Facilities:** "Fund based limit is INR1,300 crores out of that INR530 crores is term loans and balance INR800
  crores is EC [cash credit]." Non-fund-based INR5,000cr. Utilisation: "fund based is 39% utilised, non-fund based 65%."
- **No dilution planned:** fund raise "Not for the moment."
- **Buyback flagged by a shareholder, acknowledged not committed.** Investor: "There were a market cap of the company,
  about INR3,800 cores… You also have a net cash your balance sheet is very strong why don't you think of some
  buyback?" Management: "there is lot of capital infusion that the company is doing and for the capex. So currently we
  also understand and we know that it's a highly lucrative thing… but currently we are just waiting for some time but
  yes it's on our cards."
- **Non-core asset sale funding the gap:** Vizag INR180cr / 30-acre deal signed, cash in Q2–Q3.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Guidance credibility is the central risk.** An analyst put it directly: "last year's quarter 1 concall guidance was
  of 15% top line growth as well and yet revenue was flat and 2% this quarter." The FY27 guide now requires roughly
  20%+ growth across 9M — management accepted the arithmetic ("in next three quarters we need close to a 20% kind of
  execution growth… Yes, Shravan").
- **The FY28 INR7,500cr target has already slipped one year** from FY27 — "so it will be late by 1 year."
- **Root cause of the FY26 miss is structural to their order type, not one-off:** "big ticket size projects which did
  not take off due to the land acquisition issues, tree-cutting permissions and finalization of GAD… sometimes it
  happens faster, sometimes it takes a bit longer time." GMLR needed "Supreme Court permission, we got the permission
  in August '25."
- **BMC water-usage ban** — flagged in the opening remarks as a named drag ("most notably the restrictions imposed by
  the BMC on water usage at construction sites. This temporary ban has slowed progress on certain projects") but
  resolved by the call: "It was a temporary issue Rahul. It's already sorted and things are on track."
- **Monsoon extension risk** on earthwork-heavy sites: "where the earthwork cannot be done in rains" (Vadhvan);
  mitigated by geographic spread ("Delhi also, Chennai also, the monsoons are differently in different states").
- **DMRC INR1,500cr L1 hinges on World Bank clearances** — outside management's control.
- **Vadhvan land acquisition still sits with government** on the initial 6–7km from the port.
- **Working capital and gross debt both moved the wrong way QoQ** (103 vs 99 days; INR840cr vs ~INR580cr), though both
  are explained and guided back.
- **Named external factor with no quantification:** "growth during the quarter was tempered by external factors,
  including the U.S. Iran war." No number attached — do not size it.

**Qualifying near-term triggers (≤2, per SPEC §10):**
1. **GMLR TBM-1 launch + INR300cr capitalisation — Aug 2026, Commissioning, impact High.** "the first TBM is ready for
   launch for drilling in the ground physically… as soon as we get a go ahead, any time Monday or Tuesday" and "once
   the TBM is starting in the next 2, 3 days or so, the TBM of INR300 crores will be capitalized." Unlocks the
   INR3,000–4,000cr GMLR tunnelling revenue stream and simultaneously steps depreciation INR50cr→INR60cr/quarter.
2. **DMRC INR1,500cr underground order conversion — Q2FY27 (Jul–Sep 2026), Order-conversion, impact High.** "when this
   DMRC order is likely to be converted in Q3? — In Q2, not even Q3. We have just gone with Q1. So Q2, we will surely
   get that order." Single order ≈ a quarter of the guided FY27 revenue base of ~INR6,500cr.

*(Considered and excluded: Vizag INR180cr monetisation — dated to "Q2, Q3" but sized below the impact bar vs the
company; FY27 inflow guide of INR8,000–10,000cr — a target, not a hard-dated conversion; TBM-2 launch "in the next
2 months" — same event-family as trigger 1.)*

bull_bear.body:
Unusually plain-spoken about their own miss. Rather than defend the FY27 INR7,500cr target they retired it on the call
("our target of INR7,500 crores for FY27 is now shifted to FY28"), and they named the FY26 causes without hedging
("all these projects could not see the light of sun"). The stated operating philosophy is margin-first and was
repeated unprompted: "Unless we make margins, we don't want growth. We don't want to become a follow company where we
don't have margins and we are just doing top lines and making everyone a rosy picture." On intake they deliberately
under-committed: "we really don't want to overcome it. **We want to over deliver and then speak**… let's talk, I think
after Q2, it could be a better time when we can speak about it." Against that, the same 15% growth guide has now been
given two years running with a flat year in between — the tone is credible, the forecasting record is not yet.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- **The company is net cash (−INR45cr) while gross debt rose to INR840cr.** The surplus is parked in debt securities
  and FDs held as bank margin, which is what produces the INR19cr "recurring" other income — so a visible slice of the
  INR97cr PAT is non-operating and would compress if that cash is deployed into the guided execution ramp.
- **The mobilisation advance is not free float.** All INR470cr is interest-bearing at 8.5–10% — the usual EPC
  assumption that advances subsidise working capital does not apply here.
- **The "metro company" label is now stale.** Metro (elevated + underground) is **9%** of the book against 16% at
  Mar'25 (per our Q4FY25 note), while elevated corridors/flyovers hold 48% and "others" has doubled to 23%. The
  DMRC L1 and the stadium/sports work are what would rebuild the metro and building mix.
- **The TBM capitalisation cuts both ways in the same quarter** — it is a P&L cost (dep INR50→60cr/qtr) *and* the
  stated fix for the 29.7% tax rate ("will give shelter to the tax").
- **Chennai's delay was monetised, not absorbed** — "we have also taken a prolongation cost from them and they have
  paid us that as well… No impact on the margins." A claim actually collected is rare in this sector and is a quiet
  quality-of-client signal.
- **The binding capacity constraint is the INR5,000cr non-fund-based limit at 65% utilisation**, not equity —
  which is consistent with the fund raise being shelved and a buyback being "on our cards."
- **FY27 intake is the genuine inflection, not FY27 revenue.** By their own admission "last year we didn't have a very
  great number that we could book"; INR7,000cr in a single quarter against an INR8,000–10,000cr full-year guide resets
  the FY28–FY29 revenue base regardless of how FY27 execution lands.

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Working capital and receivables risk — Project delays, cost overruns and consequent delays in customer collections could increase working capital intensity and adversely impact liquidity and the cash flow profile. Mitigation rests on close client coordination for timely project certifications, approvals and collections; the working capital cycle improved from 112 days in FY 2024-25 to 99 days in FY 2025-26. BRSR also flags financial and working capital management as a material issue, since large infrastructure projects require substantial capital.
- Competition risk - relaxed bidding norms and aggressive pricing — Heightened competitive intensity, driven by relaxed bidding norms and aggressive pricing by new market participants, could hurt order-book growth and compress margins. The Company responds with a disciplined, margin-accretive bidding approach, selectively pursuing opportunities aligned to its core capabilities, backed by its execution record, geographic footprint and investment in specialised equipment.
- Project execution and timely delivery — Delays in project execution can lead to cost overruns and reputational damage (BRSR material issue 13). Mitigation is stronger project management practice, real-time progress monitoring, efficient resource allocation and prompt identification of bottlenecks.
- Raw material price volatility — Volatility in cement, bricks, sand and steel prices, particularly amid ongoing geopolitical tensions, could raise input costs and pressure margins. Long-standing supplier relationships and an entrenched procurement network provide sourcing resilience, and price variation clauses across project contracts allow eligible cost escalations to be passed through.
- Human resource risk - skilled labour shortage and attrition — Labour shortages and difficulty recruiting and retaining skilled talent could hurt project execution, operational efficiency and the ability to sustain the growth trajectory. BRSR material issue 2 adds that disputes and high attrition, especially among skilled staff, can hit project timelines. Mitigation is capability building, talent acquisition and retention, engagement and defined succession planning.
- Finance risk - funding availability and cost — Inability to meet funding requirements or secure financing on favourable terms could delay project execution, raise financing costs and hurt profitability. The Company points to a cash balance of `235 crore as of March 31, 2026, a gross debt-to-equity ratio improved from 0.23x to 0.18x, and credit ratings for fund-based and non-fund-based facilities upgraded to A+ Positive.
- Economic slowdown risk — An economic slowdown may affect overall business operations and result in extended project timelines; the Company's counterweight is the Government's continued emphasis on infrastructure creation and modernisation, which it treats as a tailwind for growth.
- Quality and technology obsolescence risk — Any lapse in stringent quality standards could damage reputation and impair prospects for winning future projects, while use of obsolete or outdated technologies could slow execution, reduce efficiency and hurt project economics. Mitigation is quality assurance and material validation across the project lifecycle backed by ISO 9001:2015 certification, plus continued investment in advanced construction equipment, digital project monitoring platforms and process-oriented systems.
- Occupational health and safety exposure — BRSR material issue 1: high-risk infrastructure activities necessitate robust safety measures, with negative financial implications if they fail. The Company cites ISO 45001 adoption and a PDCA framework, monthly HSE reviews, regular safety audits, Job Safety Analysis for high-risk tasks and enhanced site safety training.

business.body:
- **GMLR (Goregaon–Mulund Link Road) — the swing project.** "GMLR has gone to 26%." Casting is ahead of boring:
  "yesterday, we completed 2,000 links of casting. That's around 4 kilometers of tunnel has been casted in the casting
  yard." TBM-1: "the first TBM is ready for launch for drilling in the ground physically. So we are just waiting for a
  confirmation from the political teams, Chief Minister and ECM." TBM-2: "in advanced stage of getting assembled. So in
  the next 2 months' time, we should be able to launch that machine also." Revenue significance: "in next 2 years,
  we'll finish the whole tunnelling. So close to around INR3,000 crores, INR4,000 crores worth of top line will be
  achieved from that project." Schedule was rescued, not extended: "we are entitled for 2 years extension, but we won't
  be requiring it… the work which had to be done in 18 months, we have done in 10 months."
- **Chennai (five packages).** State package: "costing INR580 crores, which is like almost 65% completed. So we plan to
  hand over it by March 2027." Central: "four packages of National Highway Authority costing INR3,570 crores… we plan
  to complete that by December 28 now." Overall "Percentage execution of Chennai is around 20%." Delay cause and — the
  notable part — the remedy: "21 kilometer is in the Cooum river… NHAI has already given us the extension for that…
  we have also **taken a prolongation cost from them and they have paid us that as well**." Margin impact: "No impact
  on the margins, yes."
- **Anand Nagar–Saket (Mulund).** "We have completed around 15%… we intend to complete the same in scheduled date of
  October 28." The withheld frontage is now released: "the initial 2.5 kilometres stretch of NHAI was not handed over
  because of that between NHAI and MMRDA, there's some decision to be taken for toll and all… it is sorted now. So we
  have got that 3 kilometres also out of 8.5 kilometres."
- **VDCR (Versova–Dahisar Coastal Road) — the identified laggard.** "there is VDCR which is a little bit slow. And we
  expect that in a month or 2 months max time, we will be able to push that project also fully on track because the
  GAD is finalized, the land acquisition processes are done… From quarter 3, we should be able to see good push."
  Carries a claim upside: "there is a positive upside COS also that is happening in VDCR."
- **Vadhvan — greenfield, back-ended.** "our mobilisation is going on in full swing but because of rains not much can
  be done and there are some land acquisition to be done by the government… tree cutting permissions have been obtained
  from forest… the actual excavation and this work will be started only in October." Land exposure is localised:
  "initial stretch of 32 kilometres long so initial I think around 6 kilometers, 7 kilometres stretch from the port
  there is some land acquisition issue, not in the entire stretch." Revenue: "Vadhvan project revenue will start
  kicking off only from quarter 3."
- **Godrej project.** "Godrej also had some land acquisition issues, but it's like part portion of. It, not even
  like 20%."
- **New FY27 orders' contribution is deliberately small this year:** "it can be 500 or 400 or can be 600 that depends,
  but of course good revenue will come out of these new models also in this year as well."

- **Equipment capex as an entry barrier on the complex jobs.** "this GMLR project required a big capex of like INR400

  project, we required special guarantee and special launchers. So we had a capex of around INR350 crores, INR400
  crores there." The corollary is operating leverage on repeats: "all other projects does not require big capex because
  they are repeat things and we already have that capex of the equipment."
- **Bonding capacity, not equity, is the real EPC licence.** Non-fund-based limit "is INR5,000 crores", 65% utilised;
  fund-based INR1,300cr at 39% utilised.
- **Client quality insulates the cash cycle** where peers are stressed: "with DMRC, MMRDA, MSRDC, BMC, NHAI, there is
  absolutely no issue and we are getting prompt payments from them. So it's quite regular cash flow."
- **Demonstrated schedule compression.** "the work which had to be done in 18 months, we have done in 10 months. So the
  TBM was as per the key date, it has to be done 18 months from the date of site handing over, which we are completing
  in 10, 11 months."
- **Stated willingness to forgo revenue for price** — a moat only if it holds: "if we don't get a work at our margins,
  we will join hands and come to investors that we didn't get work according to our margins… We will keep our topline
  flat… As far as you don't have margins there is no use of doing business."

business.body: Founded in 1980 by Mr. Jagdishkumar M. Gupta and incorporated in 1999, JKIL builds urban infrastructure under Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) and Design-and-Build models, with construction accounting for 100% of turnover. Its customers are almost entirely government and public-sector bodies - metro rail corporations, municipal corporations, public works departments, urban development and transport authorities - including NHAI, MMRDA, DMRC, MSRDC, CIDCO Metro, Maha Metro, ESIC, UPRNL, Central and Western Railways and RVNL. A workforce of 6,955 people, including more than 1,100 engineers across planning, design coordination, construction management, quality, safety and commercial control, supports more than 40 ongoing projects across the country.

outlook.body:
- Selectivity before the bid: JKIL prefers complex urban infrastructure where technical capability supports better project control and margin protection, and avoids regular exposure to capital-heavy BOT models, staying with EPC contracts
- S1 - Choose projects where capability matters: continue focusing on metro infrastructure, elevated corridors, bridges, road tunnels, coastal connectors, institutional buildings and water infrastructure, the categories that match the equipment base, technical teams and delivery history (around 80% of the order book sits in elevated corridors, roads/tunnels and metro)
- S2 - Protect bid quality: hold a disciplined EBITDA margin filter of around 14-15% for new orders, accepting muted order inflow rather than adding low-return work
- S3 - Build for the next technical frontier: invest upfront in TBM-led tunnelling, coastal/elevated projects, large casting yards and complex metro work as the market shifts towards underground and high-barrier projects
- S4 - Convert work into cash: keep project planning, client coordination, billing documentation and collections advancing in sync in a milestone-linked EPC model
- S5 - Deepen relationships with public authorities: build on the base across MMRDA, DMRC, MMRC, NHAI, CIDCO, BMC, PMRDA, NBCC and other government clients for long-term opportunity and better counterparty visibility
- S6 - Scale systems before scaling revenue: strengthen planning, safety, people capability, environmental tracking, procurement discipline and governance so the Company scales without weakening operating control
- Apply the FY 2025-26 bid filters to the FY 2026-27 pipeline - a project must fit the engineering capability, offer workable commercial terms, carry acceptable counterparty and approval risk, and justify the equipment and working capital it will absorb
- FY 2026-27 execution priorities: accelerate GMLR, Chennai, Versova-Dahisar, Ulwe and other large projects; bring physical progress, measurement and certification closer together; replenish the order book within margin standards; and strengthen people, safety systems and project controls for a larger execution base
- Keep borrowings controlled, supported by the cash-positive balance sheet and the improved working capital cycle
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Capital expenditure during FY 2025-26 was around `500 crore, directed primarily at the GMLR TBMs, the Chennai casting yard and fleet requirements - capital pointed at visible project requirements rather than speculative capacity. FY 2026-27 capital expenditure is expected at `200-250 crore, largely for maintenance, residual project equipment and upcoming requirements, with borrowings expected to remain controlled on the back of the cash-positive balance sheet and the improved working capital cycle. The stated FY 2026-27 operating priorities are to accelerate GMLR, Chennai, Versova-Dahisar, Ulwe and other large projects, bring physical progress, measurement and certification closer together, replenish the order book within margin standards, and strengthen the people, safety systems and project controls required for a larger execution base; management notes several large projects now have the approvals, equipment, teams and workfronts needed to support higher activity. On the order side, the Company held L1 positions worth `2,490 crore taking combined visibility close to `25,000 crore, and is targeting FY 2026-27 order intake of `8,000-10,000 crore against a near-term bid pipeline of `15,000-20,000 crore, with opportunities visible across Mumbai Metro Lines 5, 10, 13 and 14, Delhi and Pune Metro, elevated corridors and projects linked to MMRDA and MSRDC. outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Public capex is the base layer of demand - FY 2026-27 public capital expenditure proposed at `12.2 lakh crore (against `11.2 lakh crore in Union Budget 2025-26), which matters directly because JKIL's client base is primarily public sector and government-backed authorities
- Urban mobility moving to networked systems - metro coverage grew to more than 1,000 km of operational network across more than 20 cities by 2025, with the opportunity now in extensions, interchange lines, airport links, underground packages, depot works, elevated corridors and integration with wider city transport
- Elevated corridors becoming city decongestion tools - large cities need elevated connectors, coastal roads, creek bridges, airport links and multi-modal access corridors that improve travel flows without acquiring vast new surface land; this is JKIL's largest order-book segment at around 51%
- Tunnelling becoming a higher-barrier opportunity as denser cities push infrastructure below the surface, creating a specialist growth area for firms that can manage equipment, geology, safety, lining, ventilation interfaces and round-the-clock engineering controls
- Airport-linked and coastal connectivity gaining strategic value - the Atal Setu, Navi Mumbai International Airport and the wider MMR programme are raising the importance of last-mile and cross-region connectors built around ecology, settlements and coastal regulations
- Water and civic infrastructure diversifying the portfolio - sewage systems, riverfront renewal, water utility tunnels and civic assets that improve liveability and environmental resilience
- The operating reality that gates revenue conversion: FY 2025-26 showed the difference between order-book size and revenue conversion, with execution delayed by monsoon intensity, regulatory approvals, land handover, environmental permissions, milestone-linked billing and client-side sequencing
- Revenue mix in FY 2025-26: metro infrastructure 29% of revenue (11% underground, 18% elevated), elevated corridors and flyovers another 29%, roads and tunnels 25%, and water, civil and other projects the remaining 17%
- Margin narrative: management states new jobs secured continue to be in a similar 14-15% margin band, with FY 2025-26 EBITDA margin steady at 14.4%
- Cash conversion is improving - operating cash flow of `1,128 crore and working capital days down to 99, strengthening the cash base for the next execution cycle
- Several large projects now have the approvals, equipment, teams and workfronts needed to support higher activity, and post-year-end order wins improve future visibility, giving room to mobilise without stretching the balance sheet
- Policy frameworks cited as demand scaffolding: the National Infrastructure Pipeline (1,261 projects, US$2,689.46 billion total project cost), PM Gati Shakti (US$1.3 trillion planned outlay), Bharatmala, Sagarmala, PMGSY and the Smart Cities Mission carried forward through the Urban Challenge Fund, which the Company says is deepening the pipeline for redevelopment, sanitation, mobility, digital infrastructure and climate-resilient civic assets
- Demographic and investment pull: population estimated at 1.46 billion in 2025 with the urban share rising to 37.1%, and record FDI inflows of US$73.7 billion in the first nine months of FY 2025-26, reinforcing the need for continued infrastructure development
- Order book at March 31, 2026 stood at `18,554 crore
- Order-book mix: elevated corridors and flyovers around 51%, roads and road tunnels 18%, metro projects 11%, and civil and other infrastructure 20%
- Around 80% of the order book is concentrated in elevated corridors, roads/tunnels and metro projects - the categories where JKIL has the deepest operational experience
- Fresh inflow during FY 2025-26 remained modest as tendering slowed and the Company held its pricing thresholds; contracts awarded worth `1,039 crore in FY 2026
- FY 2025-26 order wins named in the MD&A financial review: Multi-modal Integration Facilities at 8 Metro Stations of Mumbai Metro Line 4 & 4A (Pkg-1) for MMRDA (Maharashtra); a Foot Over Bridge for Mumbai Metro Line 4 and 4A at Pant Nagar, Vikhroli including Vijay Garden Metro Station (Package 2) for MMRDA (Maharashtra); and the twin tunnel from Film City Goregaon to Khindipada (Amar Nagar) Mulund including a Box Tunnel (Cut & Cover) at Film City for BMC (Maharashtra)
- Order momentum improved sharply after year end - by May 2026 JKIL had secured orders worth `4,556 crore and held L1 positions worth `2,490 crore, taking combined visibility close to `25,000 crore, with the new work including a Delhi Metro package and orders in core urban infrastructure
- For FY 2026-27 the Company is targeting order intake of `8,000-10,000 crore against a near-term bid pipeline of `15,000-20,000 crore
- Opportunities are visible across Mumbai Metro Lines 5, 10, 13 and 14, Delhi and Pune Metro, elevated corridors, and projects linked to MMRDA and MSRDC
- Revenue and order book have grown at a CAGR of 11% over 2008-2026

A soft print (revenue +2%, EBITDA −1%, PAT −6%) that management frames as the tail of a two-year approvals
logjam rather than a demand problem — the fix is visible: GMLR is at 26% with the first TBM "ready for launch",
VDCR's GAD and land acquisition are finally closed, and Vadhvan starts excavating in October. The real change
this quarter is intake, not execution: INR7,000cr booked/L1 in Q1 alone against a full-year guide of
INR8,000–10,000cr, after a FY26 in which "we didn't have a very great number that we could book." The cost of the
candour is that the INR7,500cr top-line target has been explicitly pushed from FY27 to FY28, and the 15% FY27
growth guide now requires ~20%+ execution growth across the remaining three quarters.

risks.note: Project delays, cost overruns and consequent delays in customer collections could increase working capital intensity and adversely impact liquidity and the cash flow profile. Mitigation rests on close client coordination for timely project certifications, approvals and collections; the working capital cycle improved from 112 days in FY 2024-25 to 99 days in FY 2025-26. BRSR also flags financial and working capital management as a material issue, since large infrastructure projects require substantial capital.

Heightened competitive intensity, driven by relaxed bidding norms and aggressive pricing by new market participants, could hurt order-book growth and compress margins. The Company responds with a disciplined, margin-accretive bidding approach, selectively pursuing opportunities aligned to its core capabilities, backed by its execution record, geographic footprint and investment in specialised equipment.
risks.risk: Competition risk - relaxed bidding norms and aggressive pricing

risks.note: Delays in project execution can lead to cost overruns and reputational damage (BRSR material issue 13). Mitigation is stronger project management practice, real-time progress monitoring, efficient resource allocation and prompt identification of bottlenecks.

Volatility in cement, bricks, sand and steel prices, particularly amid ongoing geopolitical tensions, could raise input costs and pressure margins. Long-standing supplier relationships and an entrenched procurement network provide sourcing resilience, and price variation clauses across project contracts allow eligible cost escalations to be passed through.

Labour shortages and difficulty recruiting and retaining skilled talent could hurt project execution, operational efficiency and the ability to sustain the growth trajectory. BRSR material issue 2 adds that disputes and high attrition, especially among skilled staff, can hit project timelines. Mitigation is capability building, talent acquisition and retention, engagement and defined succession planning.
risks.risk: Human resource risk - skilled labour shortage and attrition

risks.note: Inability to meet funding requirements or secure financing on favourable terms could delay project execution, raise financing costs and hurt profitability. The Company points to a cash balance of `235 crore as of March 31, 2026, a gross debt-to-equity ratio improved from 0.23x to 0.18x, and credit ratings for fund-based and non-fund-based facilities upgraded to A+ Positive.
risks.risk: Finance risk - funding availability and cost

risks.note: An economic slowdown may affect overall business operations and result in extended project timelines; the Company's counterweight is the Government's continued emphasis on infrastructure creation and modernisation, which it treats as a tailwind for growth.

Any lapse in stringent quality standards could damage reputation and impair prospects for winning future projects, while use of obsolete or outdated technologies could slow execution, reduce efficiency and hurt project economics. Mitigation is quality assurance and material validation across the project lifecycle backed by ISO 9001:2015 certification, plus continued investment in advanced construction equipment, digital project monitoring platforms and process-oriented systems.

risks.note: Project delays, cost overruns and consequent delays in customer collections could increase working capital intensity and adversely impact liquidity and the cash flow profile. Mitigation rests on close client coordination for timely project certifications, approvals and collections; the working capital cycle improved from 112 days in FY 2024-25 to 99 days in FY 2025-26. BRSR also flags financial and working capital management as a material issue, since large infrastructure projects require substantial capital.

risks.risk: Competition risk - relaxed bidding norms and aggressive pricing
risks.note: Heightened competitive intensity, driven by relaxed bidding norms and aggressive pricing by new market participants, could hurt order-book growth and compress margins. The Company responds with a disciplined, margin-accretive bidding approach, selectively pursuing opportunities aligned to its core capabilities, backed by its execution record, geographic footprint and investment in specialised equipment.

Delays in project execution can lead to cost overruns and reputational damage (BRSR material issue 13). Mitigation is stronger project management practice, real-time progress monitoring, efficient resource allocation and prompt identification of bottlenecks.

Volatility in cement, bricks, sand and steel prices, particularly amid ongoing geopolitical tensions, could raise input costs and pressure margins. Long-standing supplier relationships and an entrenched procurement network provide sourcing resilience, and price variation clauses across project contracts allow eligible cost escalations to be passed through.

risks.risk: Human resource risk - skilled labour shortage and attrition
risks.note: Labour shortages and difficulty recruiting and retaining skilled talent could hurt project execution, operational efficiency and the ability to sustain the growth trajectory. BRSR material issue 2 adds that disputes and high attrition, especially among skilled staff, can hit project timelines. Mitigation is capability building, talent acquisition and retention, engagement and defined succession planning.

risks.risk: Finance risk - funding availability and cost
risks.note: Inability to meet funding requirements or secure financing on favourable terms could delay project execution, raise financing costs and hurt profitability. The Company points to a cash balance of `235 crore as of March 31, 2026, a gross debt-to-equity ratio improved from 0.23x to 0.18x, and credit ratings for fund-based and non-fund-based facilities upgraded to A+ Positive.

An economic slowdown may affect overall business operations and result in extended project timelines; the Company's counterweight is the Government's continued emphasis on infrastructure creation and modernisation, which it treats as a tailwind for growth.

Any lapse in stringent quality standards could damage reputation and impair prospects for winning future projects, while use of obsolete or outdated technologies could slow execution, reduce efficiency and hurt project economics. Mitigation is quality assurance and material validation across the project lifecycle backed by ISO 9001:2015 certification, plus continued investment in advanced construction equipment, digital project monitoring platforms and process-oriented systems.

BRSR material issue 1: high-risk infrastructure activities necessitate robust safety measures, with negative financial implications if they fail. The Company cites ISO 45001 adoption and a PDCA framework, monthly HSE reviews, regular safety audits, Job Safety Analysis for high-risk tasks and enhanced site safety training.

one-line thesis:
A soft print (revenue +2%, EBITDA −1%, PAT −6%) that management frames as the tail of a two-year approvals
logjam rather than a demand problem — the fix is visible: GMLR is at 26% with the first TBM "ready for launch",
VDCR's GAD and land acquisition are finally closed, and Vadhvan starts excavating in October. The real change
this quarter is intake, not execution: INR7,000cr booked/L1 in Q1 alone against a full-year guide of
INR8,000–10,000cr, after a FY26 in which "we didn't have a very great number that we could book." The cost of the
candour is that the INR7,500cr top-line target has been explicitly pushed from FY27 to FY28, and the 15% FY27
growth guide now requires ~20%+ execution growth across the remaining three quarters.

  happens faster, sometimes it takes a bit longer time." GMLR needed "Supreme Court permission, we got the permission
  in August '25."
- **BMC water-usage ban** — flagged in the opening remarks as a named drag ("most notably the restrictions imposed by
  the BMC on water usage at construction sites. This temporary ban has slowed progress on certain projects") but
  resolved by the call: "It was a temporary issue Rahul. It's already sorted and things are on track."
- **Monsoon extension risk** on earthwork-heavy sites: "where the earthwork cannot be done in rains" (Vadhvan);
  mitigated by geographic spread ("Delhi also, Chennai also, the monsoons are differently in different states").
- **DMRC INR1,500cr L1 hinges on World Bank clearances** — outside management's control.
- **Vadhvan land acquisition still sits with government** on the initial 6–7km from the port.
- **Working capital and gross debt both moved the wrong way QoQ** (103 vs 99 days; INR840cr vs ~INR580cr), though both
  are explained and guided back.
- **Named external factor with no quantification:** "growth during the quarter was tempered by external factors,
  including the U.S. Iran war." No number attached — do not size it.

**Qualifying near-term triggers (≤2, per SPEC §10):**
1. **GMLR TBM-1 launch + INR300cr capitalisation — Aug 2026, Commissioning, impact High.** "the first TBM is ready for
   launch for drilling in the ground physically… as soon as we get a go ahead, any time Monday or Tuesday" and "once
   the TBM is starting in the next 2, 3 days or so, the TBM of INR300 crores will be capitalized." Unlocks the
   INR3,000–4,000cr GMLR tunnelling revenue stream and simultaneously steps depreciation INR50cr→INR60cr/quarter.
2. **DMRC INR1,500cr underground order conversion — Q2FY27 (Jul–Sep 2026), Order-conversion, impact High.** "when this
   DMRC order is likely to be converted in Q3? — In Q2, not even Q3. We have just gone with Q1. So Q2, we will surely
   get that order." Single order ≈ a quarter of the guided FY27 revenue base of ~INR6,500cr.

*(Considered and excluded: Vizag INR180cr monetisation — dated to "Q2, Q3" but sized below the impact bar vs the
company; FY27 inflow guide of INR8,000–10,000cr — a target, not a hard-dated conversion; TBM-2 launch "in the next
2 months" — same event-family as trigger 1.)*
management quality / tone:
Unusually plain-spoken about their own miss. Rather than defend the FY27 INR7,500cr target they retired it on the call
("our target of INR7,500 crores for FY27 is now shifted to FY28"), and they named the FY26 causes without hedging
("all these projects could not see the light of sun"). The stated operating philosophy is margin-first and was
repeated unprompted: "Unless we make margins, we don't want growth. We don't want to become a follow company where we
don't have margins and we are just doing top lines and making everyone a rosy picture." On intake they deliberately
under-committed: "we really don't want to overcome it. **We want to over deliver and then speak**… let's talk, I think
after Q2, it could be a better time when we can speak about it." Against that, the same 15% growth guide has now been
given two years running with a flat year in between — the tone is credible, the forecasting record is not yet.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The company is net cash (−INR45cr) while gross debt rose to INR840cr.** The surplus is parked in debt securities
  and FDs held as bank margin, which is what produces the INR19cr "recurring" other income — so a visible slice of the
  INR97cr PAT is non-operating and would compress if that cash is deployed into the guided execution ramp.
- **The mobilisation advance is not free float.** All INR470cr is interest-bearing at 8.5–10% — the usual EPC
  assumption that advances subsidise working capital does not apply here.
- **The "metro company" label is now stale.** Metro (elevated + underground) is **9%** of the book against 16% at
  Mar'25 (per our Q4FY25 note), while elevated corridors/flyovers hold 48% and "others" has doubled to 23%. The
  DMRC L1 and the stadium/sports work are what would rebuild the metro and building mix.
- **The TBM capitalisation cuts both ways in the same quarter** — it is a P&L cost (dep INR50→60cr/qtr) *and* the
  stated fix for the 29.7% tax rate ("will give shelter to the tax").
- **Chennai's delay was monetised, not absorbed** — "we have also taken a prolongation cost from them and they have
  paid us that as well… No impact on the margins." A claim actually collected is rare in this sector and is a quiet
  quality-of-client signal.
- **The binding capacity constraint is the INR5,000cr non-fund-based limit at 65% utilisation**, not equity —
  which is consistent with the fund raise being shelved and a buyback being "on our cards."
- **FY27 intake is the genuine inflection, not FY27 revenue.** By their own admission "last year we didn't have a very
  great number that we could book"; INR7,000cr in a single quarter against an INR8,000–10,000cr full-year guide resets
  the FY28–FY29 revenue base regardless of how FY27 execution lands.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: J. Kumar Infraprojects is one of India's leading EPC companies in complex urban infrastructure - underground and elevated metros, flyovers, bridges, expressways, road tunnels, riverfronts and water systems - carrying a total order book of `18,554 crore as on March 31, 2026.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Founded in 1980 by Mr. Jagdishkumar M. Gupta and incorporated in 1999, JKIL builds urban infrastructure under Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) and Design-and-Build models, with construction accounting for 100% of turnover. Its customers are almost entirely government and public-sector bodies - metro rail corporations, municipal corporations, public works departments, urban development and transport authorities - including NHAI, MMRDA, DMRC, MSRDC, CIDCO Metro, Maha Metro, ESIC, UPRNL, Central and Western Railways and RVNL. A workforce of 6,955 people, including more than 1,100 engineers across planning, design coordination, construction management, quality, safety and commercial control, supports more than 40 ongoing projects across the country.

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail
segment_detail.body:
- **GMLR (Goregaon–Mulund Link Road) — the swing project.** "GMLR has gone to 26%." Casting is ahead of boring:
  "yesterday, we completed 2,000 links of casting. That's around 4 kilometers of tunnel has been casted in the casting
  yard." TBM-1: "the first TBM is ready for launch for drilling in the ground physically. So we are just waiting for a
  confirmation from the political teams, Chief Minister and ECM." TBM-2: "in advanced stage of getting assembled. So in
  the next 2 months' time, we should be able to launch that machine also." Revenue significance: "in next 2 years,
  we'll finish the whole tunnelling. So close to around INR3,000 crores, INR4,000 crores worth of top line will be
  achieved from that project." Schedule was rescued, not extended: "we are entitled for 2 years extension, but we won't
  be requiring it… the work which had to be done in 18 months, we have done in 10 months."
- **Chennai (five packages).** State package: "costing INR580 crores, which is like almost 65% completed. So we plan to
  hand over it by March 2027." Central: "four packages of National Highway Authority costing INR3,570 crores… we plan
  to complete that by December 28 now." Overall "Percentage execution of Chennai is around 20%." Delay cause and — the
  notable part — the remedy: "21 kilometer is in the Cooum river… NHAI has already given us the extension for that…
  we have also **taken a prolongation cost from them and they have paid us that as well**." Margin impact: "No impact
  on the margins, yes."
- **Anand Nagar–Saket (Mulund).** "We have completed around 15%… we intend to complete the same in scheduled date of
  October 28." The withheld frontage is now released: "the initial 2.5 kilometres stretch of NHAI was not handed over
  because of that between NHAI and MMRDA, there's some decision to be taken for toll and all… it is sorted now. So we
  have got that 3 kilometres also out of 8.5 kilometres."
- **VDCR (Versova–Dahisar Coastal Road) — the identified laggard.** "there is VDCR which is a little bit slow. And we
  expect that in a month or 2 months max time, we will be able to push that project also fully on track because the
  GAD is finalized, the land acquisition processes are done… From quarter 3, we should be able to see good push."
  Carries a claim upside: "there is a positive upside COS also that is happening in VDCR."
- **Vadhvan — greenfield, back-ended.** "our mobilisation is going on in full swing but because of rains not much can
  be done and there are some land acquisition to be done by the government… tree cutting permissions have been obtained
  from forest… the actual excavation and this work will be started only in October." Land exposure is localised:
  "initial stretch of 32 kilometres long so initial I think around 6 kilometers, 7 kilometres stretch from the port
  there is some land acquisition issue, not in the entire stretch." Revenue: "Vadhvan project revenue will start
  kicking off only from quarter 3."
- **Godrej project.** "Godrej also had some land acquisition issues, but it's like part portion of. It, not even
  like 20%."
- **New FY27 orders' contribution is deliberately small this year:** "it can be 500 or 400 or can be 600 that depends,
  but of course good revenue will come out of these new models also in this year as well."

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Public capex is the base layer of demand - FY 2026-27 public capital expenditure proposed at `12.2 lakh crore (against `11.2 lakh crore in Union Budget 2025-26), which matters directly because JKIL's client base is primarily public sector and government-backed authorities
- Urban mobility moving to networked systems - metro coverage grew to more than 1,000 km of operational network across more than 20 cities by 2025, with the opportunity now in extensions, interchange lines, airport links, underground packages, depot works, elevated corridors and integration with wider city transport
- Elevated corridors becoming city decongestion tools - large cities need elevated connectors, coastal roads, creek bridges, airport links and multi-modal access corridors that improve travel flows without acquiring vast new surface land; this is JKIL's largest order-book segment at around 51%
- Tunnelling becoming a higher-barrier opportunity as denser cities push infrastructure below the surface, creating a specialist growth area for firms that can manage equipment, geology, safety, lining, ventilation interfaces and round-the-clock engineering controls
- Airport-linked and coastal connectivity gaining strategic value - the Atal Setu, Navi Mumbai International Airport and the wider MMR programme are raising the importance of last-mile and cross-region connectors built around ecology, settlements and coastal regulations
- Water and civic infrastructure diversifying the portfolio - sewage systems, riverfront renewal, water utility tunnels and civic assets that improve liveability and environmental resilience
- The operating reality that gates revenue conversion: FY 2025-26 showed the difference between order-book size and revenue conversion, with execution delayed by monsoon intensity, regulatory approvals, land handover, environmental permissions, milestone-linked billing and client-side sequencing
- Revenue mix in FY 2025-26: metro infrastructure 29% of revenue (11% underground, 18% elevated), elevated corridors and flyovers another 29%, roads and tunnels 25%, and water, civil and other projects the remaining 17%
- Margin narrative: management states new jobs secured continue to be in a similar 14-15% margin band, with FY 2025-26 EBITDA margin steady at 14.4%
- Cash conversion is improving - operating cash flow of `1,128 crore and working capital days down to 99, strengthening the cash base for the next execution cycle
- Several large projects now have the approvals, equipment, teams and workfronts needed to support higher activity, and post-year-end order wins improve future visibility, giving room to mobilise without stretching the balance sheet
- Policy frameworks cited as demand scaffolding: the National Infrastructure Pipeline (1,261 projects, US$2,689.46 billion total project cost), PM Gati Shakti (US$1.3 trillion planned outlay), Bharatmala, Sagarmala, PMGSY and the Smart Cities Mission carried forward through the Urban Challenge Fund, which the Company says is deepening the pipeline for redevelopment, sanitation, mobility, digital infrastructure and climate-resilient civic assets
- Demographic and investment pull: population estimated at 1.46 billion in 2025 with the urban share rising to 37.1%, and record FDI inflows of US$73.7 billion in the first nine months of FY 2025-26, reinforcing the need for continued infrastructure development
- Order book at March 31, 2026 stood at `18,554 crore
- Order-book mix: elevated corridors and flyovers around 51%, roads and road tunnels 18%, metro projects 11%, and civil and other infrastructure 20%
- Around 80% of the order book is concentrated in elevated corridors, roads/tunnels and metro projects - the categories where JKIL has the deepest operational experience
- Fresh inflow during FY 2025-26 remained modest as tendering slowed and the Company held its pricing thresholds; contracts awarded worth `1,039 crore in FY 2026
- FY 2025-26 order wins named in the MD&A financial review: Multi-modal Integration Facilities at 8 Metro Stations of Mumbai Metro Line 4 & 4A (Pkg-1) for MMRDA (Maharashtra); a Foot Over Bridge for Mumbai Metro Line 4 and 4A at Pant Nagar, Vikhroli including Vijay Garden Metro Station (Package 2) for MMRDA (Maharashtra); and the twin tunnel from Film City Goregaon to Khindipada (Amar Nagar) Mulund including a Box Tunnel (Cut & Cover) at Film City for BMC (Maharashtra)
- Order momentum improved sharply after year end - by May 2026 JKIL had secured orders worth `4,556 crore and held L1 positions worth `2,490 crore, taking combined visibility close to `25,000 crore, with the new work including a Delhi Metro package and orders in core urban infrastructure
- For FY 2026-27 the Company is targeting order intake of `8,000-10,000 crore against a near-term bid pipeline of `15,000-20,000 crore
- Opportunities are visible across Mumbai Metro Lines 5, 10, 13 and 14, Delhi and Pune Metro, elevated corridors, and projects linked to MMRDA and MSRDC
- Revenue and order book have grown at a CAGR of 11% over 2008-2026

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Capital expenditure during FY 2025-26 was around `500 crore, directed primarily at the GMLR TBMs, the Chennai casting yard and fleet requirements - capital pointed at visible project requirements rather than speculative capacity. FY 2026-27 capital expenditure is expected at `200-250 crore, largely for maintenance, residual project equipment and upcoming requirements, with borrowings expected to remain controlled on the back of the cash-positive balance sheet and the improved working capital cycle. The stated FY 2026-27 operating priorities are to accelerate GMLR, Chennai, Versova-Dahisar, Ulwe and other large projects, bring physical progress, measurement and certification closer together, replenish the order book within margin standards, and strengthen the people, safety systems and project controls required for a larger execution base; management notes several large projects now have the approvals, equipment, teams and workfronts needed to support higher activity. On the order side, the Company held L1 positions worth `2,490 crore taking combined visibility close to `25,000 crore, and is targeting FY 2026-27 order intake of `8,000-10,000 crore against a near-term bid pipeline of `15,000-20,000 crore, with opportunities visible across Mumbai Metro Lines 5, 10, 13 and 14, Delhi and Pune Metro, elevated corridors and projects linked to MMRDA and MSRDC. As an EPC contractor the Company discloses no manufacturing capacity, and the capital-commitments note supplied in this bundle carries no readable figure.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body:
Unusually plain-spoken about their own miss. Rather than defend the FY27 INR7,500cr target they retired it on the call
("our target of INR7,500 crores for FY27 is now shifted to FY28"), and they named the FY26 causes without hedging
("all these projects could not see the light of sun"). The stated operating philosophy is margin-first and was
repeated unprompted: "Unless we make margins, we don't want growth. We don't want to become a follow company where we
don't have margins and we are just doing top lines and making everyone a rosy picture." On intake they deliberately
under-committed: "we really don't want to overcome it. **We want to over deliver and then speak**… let's talk, I think
after Q2, it could be a better time when we can speak about it." Against that, the same 15% growth guide has now been
given two years running with a flat year in between — the tone is credible, the forecasting record is not yet.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Specialised heavy-equipment fleet - tunnel boring machines, launching girders, casting yards, RMC plants, piling equipment, segment-handling systems and heavy transport assets - which keeps critical stages of execution in-house and supports control over quality, productivity and timelines
- Deep engineering bench: more than 1,100 engineers spanning project planning, design coordination, construction management, quality, safety and commercial control, within a 6,955-person workforce
- Proven capability in the hardest project classes: India's largest TBM diameter deployed (14.42 m Rock EPB machines at the Goregaon-Mulund Link Road), a 20.9 km double-tier elevated corridor at Chennai Port-Maduravoyal, the four-level Dwarka Expressway Delhi section, and South Asia's first 100-metre-radius curved cable-stayed bridge on the Santacruz-Chembur Link Road Extension
- Credit standing: ICRA A+ / Positive rating for fund-based and non-fund-based facilities, reflecting execution record, healthy financial position, prudent leverage and strong promoter experience, which supports access to the banking facilities large EPC projects require
- Long-standing relationships with public infrastructure authorities and institutional clients, founded on technical capability, financial discipline, quality standards and a consistent record of delivery
- Portfolio concentrated in engineering-intensive segments where specialised engineering, large-scale equipment deployment and coordination across dense urban interfaces raise the barrier to entry
- Selectivity in roads - preferring technically demanding and urban or corridor-linked packages over low-margin commodity road work

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Guidance credibility is the central risk.** An analyst put it directly: "last year's quarter 1 concall guidance was
  of 15% top line growth as well and yet revenue was flat and 2% this quarter." The FY27 guide now requires roughly
  20%+ growth across 9M — management accepted the arithmetic ("in next three quarters we need close to a 20% kind of
  execution growth… Yes, Shravan").
- **The FY28 INR7,500cr target has already slipped one year** from FY27 — "so it will be late by 1 year."
- **Root cause of the FY26 miss is structural to their order type, not one-off:** "big ticket size projects which did
  not take off due to the land acquisition issues, tree-cutting permissions and finalization of GAD… sometimes it
  happens faster, sometimes it takes a bit longer time." GMLR needed "Supreme Court permission, we got the permission
  in August '25."
- **BMC water-usage ban** — flagged in the opening remarks as a named drag ("most notably the restrictions imposed by
  the BMC on water usage at construction sites. This temporary ban has slowed progress on certain projects") but
  resolved by the call: "It was a temporary issue Rahul. It's already sorted and things are on track."
- **Monsoon extension risk** on earthwork-heavy sites: "where the earthwork cannot be done in rains" (Vadhvan);
  mitigated by geographic spread ("Delhi also, Chennai also, the monsoons are differently in different states").
- **DMRC INR1,500cr L1 hinges on World Bank clearances** — outside management's control.
- **Vadhvan land acquisition still sits with government** on the initial 6–7km from the port.
- **Working capital and gross debt both moved the wrong way QoQ** (103 vs 99 days; INR840cr vs ~INR580cr), though both
  are explained and guided back.
- **Named external factor with no quantification:** "growth during the quarter was tempered by external factors,
  including the U.S. Iran war." No number attached — do not size it.

**Qualifying near-term triggers (≤2, per SPEC §10):**
1. **GMLR TBM-1 launch + INR300cr capitalisation — Aug 2026, Commissioning, impact High.** "the first TBM is ready for
   launch for drilling in the ground physically… as soon as we get a go ahead, any time Monday or Tuesday" and "once
   the TBM is starting in the next 2, 3 days or so, the TBM of INR300 crores will be capitalized." Unlocks the
   INR3,000–4,000cr GMLR tunnelling revenue stream and simultaneously steps depreciation INR50cr→INR60cr/quarter.
2. **DMRC INR1,500cr underground order conversion — Q2FY27 (Jul–Sep 2026), Order-conversion, impact High.** "when this
   DMRC order is likely to be converted in Q3? — In Q2, not even Q3. We have just gone with Q1. So Q2, we will surely
   get that order." Single order ≈ a quarter of the guided FY27 revenue base of ~INR6,500cr.

*(Considered and excluded: Vizag INR180cr monetisation — dated to "Q2, Q3" but sized below the impact bar vs the
company; FY27 inflow guide of INR8,000–10,000cr — a target, not a hard-dated conversion; TBM-2 launch "in the next
2 months" — same event-family as trigger 1.)*

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- **The company is net cash (−INR45cr) while gross debt rose to INR840cr.** The surplus is parked in debt securities
  and FDs held as bank margin, which is what produces the INR19cr "recurring" other income — so a visible slice of the
  INR97cr PAT is non-operating and would compress if that cash is deployed into the guided execution ramp.
- **The mobilisation advance is not free float.** All INR470cr is interest-bearing at 8.5–10% — the usual EPC
  assumption that advances subsidise working capital does not apply here.
- **The "metro company" label is now stale.** Metro (elevated + underground) is **9%** of the book against 16% at
  Mar'25 (per our Q4FY25 note), while elevated corridors/flyovers hold 48% and "others" has doubled to 23%. The
  DMRC L1 and the stadium/sports work are what would rebuild the metro and building mix.
- **The TBM capitalisation cuts both ways in the same quarter** — it is a P&L cost (dep INR50→60cr/qtr) *and* the
  stated fix for the 29.7% tax rate ("will give shelter to the tax").
- **Chennai's delay was monetised, not absorbed** — "we have also taken a prolongation cost from them and they have
  paid us that as well… No impact on the margins." A claim actually collected is rare in this sector and is a quiet
  quality-of-client signal.
- **The binding capacity constraint is the INR5,000cr non-fund-based limit at 65% utilisation**, not equity —
  which is consistent with the fund raise being shelved and a buyback being "on our cards."
- **FY27 intake is the genuine inflection, not FY27 revenue.** By their own admission "last year we didn't have a very
  great number that we could book"; INR7,000cr in a single quarter against an INR8,000–10,000cr full-year guide resets
  the FY28–FY29 revenue base regardless of how FY27 execution lands.

one-line thesis:
A soft print (revenue +2%, EBITDA −1%, PAT −6%) that management frames as the tail of a two-year approvals
logjam rather than a demand problem — the fix is visible: GMLR is at 26% with the first TBM "ready for launch",
VDCR's GAD and land acquisition are finally closed, and Vadhvan starts excavating in October. The real change
this quarter is intake, not execution: INR7,000cr booked/L1 in Q1 alone against a full-year guide of
INR8,000–10,000cr, after a FY26 in which "we didn't have a very great number that we could book." The cost of the
candour is that the INR7,500cr top-line target has been explicitly pushed from FY27 to FY28, and the 15% FY27
growth guide now requires ~20%+ execution growth across the remaining three quarters.

  in 10, 11 months."
- **Stated willingness to forgo revenue for price** — a moat only if it holds: "if we don't get a work at our margins,
  we will join hands and come to investors that we didn't get work according to our margins… We will keep our topline
  flat… As far as you don't have margins there is no use of doing business."
margins & cost dynamics:
- **EBITDA margin 14.1% vs 14.6% YoY**, attributed to mix and timing: "While margins moderated during the quarter,
  this was primarily attributable to the timing-related factors and the evolving mix of projects under execution."
- **Guided band 14–15%**, with a stated ambition of 15–16% ("increase by a notch 100 basis point more"). Note the FY28
  framing keeps the *lower* band: "INR7,500 crores by FY28 now with similar margins of 14% to 15% EBITDA."
- **Mobilisation advance is fully priced debt, not float.** "Mobilization advance, interest bearing portion is INR470
  crores… Total is INR470 crores… entirely it is interest [bearing]. Yes." Rate: "varying interest rate from 8.5% to
  11%", with the CFO narrowing it — "usually MCLR plus 3% plus so it's like around 8 5% to 9.5%, 10% I don't think
  anything is above 10." Blended borrowing cost: "9% to 10%."
- **Depreciation steps up** INR50cr → INR60cr per quarter on the INR300cr TBM capitalisation, on top of "last year, we
  have done capitalization of almost INR480 crores. So the full impact of that will be felt in current year."
- **Tax rate 29.7% in Q1**, expected back to the FY26 level ("more or less it should be same") once the TBM shields it.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **Q1FY27 capex INR34cr** ("capex we have done for Q1, we have done capex of INR34 crores") against a INR150cr
  full-year run-rate — front-loading has already happened.
- **Guide: "INR150 crores each year for next 2 years", inclusive of INR100cr maintenance.** The big-ticket programme is
  finished: "going forward also for a couple of two years we don't foresee any big capex coming in apart from this
  INR150 crores per year… unless and until we get some big other projects wherein some new equipment are to be
  utilized."
- **CWIP conversion is the dated event.** "as of March 26, our gross block… was around 2450 and there was CWIP of
  INR300 crores" → "in a week or so, the TBM will start. So that INR300 crores CWFP will get capitalized."
- **Slippage watch:** the entire FY27 guide leans on three October–December unlocks (TBM-1 boring, VDCR ramp from Q3,
  Vadhvan excavation from October). Any one slipping puts the 15% growth guide at risk, since Q1 delivered 2%.
capital allocation:
- **Net cash on a net-debt basis:** "Net debt is minus 45." Gross debt INR840cr vs "580 odd crores" at March, entirely
  explained by the final TBM instalment; guided "less than INR800 crores by the year end, not more" as term loan
  amortises.
- **Leverage:** "Gross debt equity is at 0.24."
- **Facilities:** "Fund based limit is INR1,300 crores out of that INR530 crores is term loans and balance INR800
  crores is EC [cash credit]." Non-fund-based INR5,000cr. Utilisation: "fund based is 39% utilised, non-fund based 65%."
- **No dilution planned:** fund raise "Not for the moment."
- **Buyback flagged by a shareholder, acknowledged not committed.** Investor: "There were a market cap of the company,
  about INR3,800 cores… You also have a net cash your balance sheet is very strong why don't you think of some
  buyback?" Management: "there is lot of capital infusion that the company is doing and for the capex. So currently we
  also understand and we know that it's a highly lucrative thing… but currently we are just waiting for some time but
  yes it's on our cards."
- **Non-core asset sale funding the gap:** Vizag INR180cr / 30-acre deal signed, cash in Q2–Q3.
risks & watch-items:
- **Guidance credibility is the central risk.** An analyst put it directly: "last year's quarter 1 concall guidance was
  of 15% top line growth as well and yet revenue was flat and 2% this quarter." The FY27 guide now requires roughly
  20%+ growth across 9M — management accepted the arithmetic ("in next three quarters we need close to a 20% kind of
  execution growth… Yes, Shravan").
- **The FY28 INR7,500cr target has already slipped one year** from FY27 — "so it will be late by 1 year."
- **Root cause of the FY26 miss is structural to their order type, not one-off:** "big ticket size projects which did
  not take off due to the land acquisition issues, tree-cutting permissions and finalization of GAD… sometimes it
  happens faster, sometimes it takes a bit longer time." GMLR needed "Supreme Court permission, we got the permission
  in August '25."
- **BMC water-usage ban** — flagged in the opening remarks as a named drag ("most notably the restrictions imposed by
  the BMC on water usage at construction sites. This temporary ban has slowed progress on certain projects") but
  resolved by the call: "It was a temporary issue Rahul. It's already sorted and things are on track."
- **Monsoon extension risk** on earthwork-heavy sites: "where the earthwork cannot be done in rains" (Vadhvan);
  mitigated by geographic spread ("Delhi also, Chennai also, the monsoons are differently in different states").
- **DMRC INR1,500cr L1 hinges on World Bank clearances** — outside management's control.
- **Vadhvan land acquisition still sits with government** on the initial 6–7km from the port.
- **Working capital and gross debt both moved the wrong way QoQ** (103 vs 99 days; INR840cr vs ~INR580cr), though both
  are explained and guided back.
- **Named external factor with no quantification:** "growth during the quarter was tempered by external factors,
  including the U.S. Iran war." No number attached — do not size it.

**Qualifying near-term triggers (≤2, per SPEC §10):**
1. **GMLR TBM-1 launch + INR300cr capitalisation — Aug 2026, Commissioning, impact High.** "the first TBM is ready for
   launch for drilling in the ground physically… as soon as we get a go ahead, any time Monday or Tuesday" and "once
   the TBM is starting in the next 2, 3 days or so, the TBM of INR300 crores will be capitalized." Unlocks the
   INR3,000–4,000cr GMLR tunnelling revenue stream and simultaneously steps depreciation INR50cr→INR60cr/quarter.
2. **DMRC INR1,500cr underground order conversion — Q2FY27 (Jul–Sep 2026), Order-conversion, impact High.** "when this
   DMRC order is likely to be converted in Q3? — In Q2, not even Q3. We have just gone with Q1. So Q2, we will surely
   get that order." Single order ≈ a quarter of the guided FY27 revenue base of ~INR6,500cr.

*(Considered and excluded: Vizag INR180cr monetisation — dated to "Q2, Q3" but sized below the impact bar vs the
company; FY27 inflow guide of INR8,000–10,000cr — a target, not a hard-dated conversion; TBM-2 launch "in the next
2 months" — same event-family as trigger 1.)*
management quality / tone:
Unusually plain-spoken about their own miss. Rather than defend the FY27 INR7,500cr target they retired it on the call
("our target of INR7,500 crores for FY27 is now shifted to FY28"), and they named the FY26 causes without hedging
("all these projects could not see the light of sun"). The stated operating philosophy is margin-first and was
repeated unprompted: "Unless we make margins, we don't want growth. We don't want to become a follow company where we
don't have margins and we are just doing top lines and making everyone a rosy picture." On intake they deliberately
under-committed: "we really don't want to overcome it. **We want to over deliver and then speak**… let's talk, I think
after Q2, it could be a better time when we can speak about it." Against that, the same 15% growth guide has now been
given two years running with a flat year in between — the tone is credible, the forecasting record is not yet.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The company is net cash (−INR45cr) while gross debt rose to INR840cr.** The surplus is parked in debt securities
  and FDs held as bank margin, which is what produces the INR19cr "recurring" other income — so a visible slice of the
  INR97cr PAT is non-operating and would compress if that cash is deployed into the guided execution ramp.
- **The mobilisation advance is not free float.** All INR470cr is interest-bearing at 8.5–10% — the usual EPC
  assumption that advances subsidise working capital does not apply here.
- **The "metro company" label is now stale.** Metro (elevated + underground) is **9%** of the book against 16% at
  Mar'25 (per our Q4FY25 note), while elevated corridors/flyovers hold 48% and "others" has doubled to 23%. The
  DMRC L1 and the stadium/sports work are what would rebuild the metro and building mix.
- **The TBM capitalisation cuts both ways in the same quarter** — it is a P&L cost (dep INR50→60cr/qtr) *and* the
  stated fix for the 29.7% tax rate ("will give shelter to the tax").
- **Chennai's delay was monetised, not absorbed** — "we have also taken a prolongation cost from them and they have
  paid us that as well… No impact on the margins." A claim actually collected is rare in this sector and is a quiet
  quality-of-client signal.
- **The binding capacity constraint is the INR5,000cr non-fund-based limit at 65% utilisation**, not equity —
  which is consistent with the fund raise being shelved and a buyback being "on our cards."
- **FY27 intake is the genuine inflection, not FY27 revenue.** By their own admission "last year we didn't have a very
  great number that we could book"; INR7,000cr in a single quarter against an INR8,000–10,000cr full-year guide resets
  the FY28–FY29 revenue base regardless of how FY27 execution lands.
